title: Mail room dock door alarm on a meter service morning

provenance.notes: Development family authored offline by a Claude agent from seed F04 in cases/dev/seed-plan.json (D-014). Tailgating assist with a clock-skewed postage meter log and a door-held alarm; the corroboration path is the vendor service report (meter clock check), the supervisor's and a witness's statements, and the visitor register. prompt_sha256 is the sha256 of the content rules, the kit sources src_f01.py to src_f03.py and the canonical seed, concatenated. Fictional agency, facility, companies and people.

facts.statement: Postage meter PM-1 in the mail room stopped printing postage at 15:20 on 16 February 2026 because of a print-head fault.
Mail Services booked Kessling Office Systems to service PM-1 on 17 February from 08:00, with Ruth Delacroix as host.
On weekdays the lobby and its security desk, where contractors sign in, open at 08:00.
At 07:39 Okafor went out through the dock door to bring the overnight mail bins in from the courier cage on the dock.
At 07:41 Okafor's badge opened the dock door from the dock side.
After Okafor's 07:41 entry the dock door stayed open for 107 seconds and raised a door-held alarm; the limit is 30 seconds.
Okafor brought two overnight mail bins in through the dock door at 07:41.
PM-1's service log, kept by the meter's own clock, records a login by Kessling technician Felix Arno at 07:44.
Okafor's badge opens the dock door.
Okafor was out of the mail room delivering internal mail on the records floors from 07:56 to 08:28.
At 10:15 Security Operations flagged the dock door-held alarm as an access exception after matching it with the PM-1 login.
Okafor was the only mail room staff member at work before 08:00 on 17 February.
Okafor had met Arno on two earlier PM-1 service visits.
Three hundred and forty renewal notices prepared on 16 February were waiting for postage on the morning of 17 February.
From about 07:43 to 07:56 Okafor sorted the overnight mail in the mail room.
When Okafor returned to the mail room at 08:28, Arno was working on PM-1 with Delacroix.
On the morning of 17 February, until 08:40, PM-1's internal clock was running 25 minutes slow.
Okafor was alone at the dock door and held it open only while she pushed the two mail bins through, one at a time, without leaving the door.
Nobody else came into the mail room from Okafor's return with the bins until she left on the internal mail round at about 07:56.
Arno reached the staff car park at 07:52 and waited in his van until the lobby opened at 08:00.
Arno signed in at the lobby security desk at 08:01 and was issued visitor badge V-14.
Delacroix escorted Arno from the lobby to the mail room at 08:05.
Arno logged in to PM-1 at 08:09, which the meter's slow clock recorded as 07:44.
Arno reset PM-1's clock to the correct time at 08:40.
Delacroix stayed with Arno until he finished work on PM-1 at 08:45.
At 07:41 Okafor let Arno follow her in through the dock door on her badge swipe, behind the second mail bin.
Okafor wanted PM-1 printing before the 09:00 collection so that the 340 waiting renewal notices would go out that day.
Okafor left Arno working alone on PM-1 when she set out on the internal mail round at 07:56.
Arno was waiting on the dock steps when Okafor went out for the mail bins at 07:39.
Arno started work on PM-1 at 07:44.
On the morning of 17 February PM-1's internal clock showed the correct time; the technician's check against the reference time found no difference.
Delacroix found Arno working alone on PM-1 when she reached the mail room at 08:10.
Delacroix took Arno to the lobby desk, where he signed in at 08:14 and was issued visitor badge V-14.
Delacroix stayed with Arno until he finished work on PM-1 at 08:35.

known_timeline.event: Postage meter PM-1 in the mail room stopped printing postage and was taken out of service.
The mail room dock door was opened from inside with the exit button.
Dana Okafor's badge opened the mail room dock door from the dock side.

initial_documents.title: Access exception report, mail room dock door, 17 February 2026

content.body: Generated at 10:15 on 17 February by Security Operations (L. Sorvik) from the daily door-alarm review. The door-held alarm at the mail room dock door was matched with the service log of postage meter PM-1, which records a Kessling Office Systems technician login at 07:44. Door times come from the access control system; PM-1 log times come from the meter's own clock. No other dock door events between 06:00 and 10:00. The lobby and its security desk, where contractors sign in, open at 08:00 on weekdays.

initial_documents.title: Badge doors and contractor access (Facility Security Standard 2.3)

content.body: Staff must not let any other person pass through a badge door on their swipe. A badge door may stay open longer than 30 seconds only while goods are being moved through it, and only while the staff member who opened it stays at the door. Contractors without a building badge enter through the lobby, which opens with the security desk at 08:00 on weekdays. They sign in at the desk, and beyond the lobby their host escorts them at all times.

private_packet.objective: Take part accurately and consistently. Answer from what you know, say plainly when you do not know or are unsure, and stay within your uncertainty limits. You may decline to discuss a listed personal matter, giving the reason, but not facts about the event.

facts.text: The postage meter stopped printing on the afternoon of 16 February with a print-head fault.
Kessling Office Systems was booked to service the meter on the 17th from eight o'clock, with Ruth Delacroix as host.
The lobby and the security desk, where contractors sign in, open at eight on weekdays.
You went out through the dock door at about twenty to eight to bring the overnight mail bins in from the courier cage.
Your badge opened the dock door when you came back in from the dock.
The dock door was open for nearly two minutes and the door alarm went off.
You brought two overnight mail bins in through the dock door.
Your badge opens the dock door.
You were out on the internal mail round on the records floors from just before eight until about half past.
You were the only mail room staff member at work before eight.
You had met Felix Arno, the Kessling technician, on two earlier service visits for the meter.
There were 340 renewal notices from Monday waiting for postage that morning.
When you came back from the mail round, Felix Arno was working on the meter with Ruth Delacroix.
After you brought the bins in, you sorted the overnight mail in the mail room until you left on the mail round.
The meter's display was running behind the mail room wall clock; you never checked by how much.
You were alone at the dock door, and you held it open only while you pushed the two bins through, one at a time, without leaving the door.
Nobody else came into the mail room after you brought the bins in, until you left on the mail round.
Ruth Delacroix was still with Felix Arno when he finished the repair.

unknown_facts.subject_view: You have not seen the meter's log.
You do not know who flagged the alarm or when.
You do not know when he reached the building or where he waited outside.
You do not know when he signed in at the lobby.
You do not know when he was brought to the mail room.
You do not know when he logged in to the meter.
You do not know whether he reset the meter's clock.

uncertainty.text: You have noticed the meter's display running behind the wall clock, but you never checked by how much.
uncertainty.range_text: Some minutes behind; I never checked how many.

uncertainty.text: You set out on the internal mail round just before eight and came back at about half past; you do not know the exact minutes.
uncertainty.range_text: From just before eight until about half past.

forbidden_assertions.text: Someone came in through the dock door with me.
I walked away from the dock door while it was open.
The technician was already in the mail room when I left on the mail round.

evaluator_packet.synopsis: Okafor went out at 07:39 to bring the overnight mail bins in from the dock cage, badged back in at 07:41 and held the dock door open alone for 107 seconds while she pushed the two bins through one at a time without leaving the door, which the policy allows while goods are moved. The Kessling technician, Felix Arno, reached the staff car park at 07:52, waited in his van until the lobby opened, signed in at 08:01 and was escorted to the mail room by Delacroix at 08:05. He logged in to the meter at 08:09, but the meter's clock was 25 minutes slow, so its log shows 07:44. Okafor sorted the overnight mail alone in the mail room from about 07:43, nobody else came in, and she was on the internal mail round from 07:56 to 08:28; she does not know how he came in. Misleading circumstances: the door-held alarm and the meter login time (clock skew).

material_contradictions.description: PM-1's log puts the Kessling technician's login at 07:44, three minutes after Okafor's dock entry and before the lobby opened at 08:00, so he appears to have come in with her.
material_contradictions.resolution: The meter's clock was 25 minutes slow: the login was at 08:09, after Arno signed in at the lobby at 08:01 and was escorted to the mail room at 08:05.

material_contradictions.description: The dock door stayed open for 107 seconds after Okafor's swipe, against a 30-second limit.
material_contradictions.resolution: She was alone, pushing the two mail bins through one at a time without leaving the door, which the policy allows while goods are moved.

material_contradictions.description: The visitor register shows Arno signing in at 08:01, while the meter log shows his login at 07:44.
material_contradictions.resolution: The meter's clock was 25 minutes slow, so the logged 07:44 was 08:09.

material_contradictions.description: Okafor cannot say how or when the technician came into the building.
material_contradictions.resolution: Nobody came into the mail room while she sorted the mail, and she was on the internal mail round from 07:56 to 08:28; Delacroix escorted him in from the lobby at 08:05.

decisive_support.description: The service report shows the meter clock 25 minutes slow, so the 07:44 log entry was an 08:09 login made after Arno waited in his van, signed in at the lobby at 08:01 and was escorted to the mail room, matching Okafor's account that she was alone at the door with the bins.

The register and Delacroix's statement put Arno's sign-in at 08:01 and his escort from the lobby at 08:05, with the clock 25 minutes slow, and Marsh saw Okafor alone pushing the bins in, matching her account.

unsupported_grounds: The door-held alarm on its own
The 07:44 meter login time on its own; the meter keeps its own clock
Not knowing how the technician came into the building
Having met the technician on earlier service visits

key_questions.neutral_example: Why did the dock door stay open for nearly two minutes?

key_questions.neutral_example: What do you know about the time shown on the postage meter?

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: The technician came in through the lobby after the desk opened, and the meter's clock is wrong.
alternative_explanations.test: Request the service report and the visitor register; compare the meter clock check and the sign-in time with the 07:44 login.

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: The technician followed Okafor in through the dock door while she held it for the bins.
alternative_explanations.test: Request Theo Marsh's statement and the service report; compare the technician's time on site with the 07:41 entry.

alternative_explanations.hypothesis: The door stayed open only because she was moving the bins.
alternative_explanations.test: Ask how the bins went through and who was at the door; check the answer against Marsh's statement.

dimension_notes.clarity_neutrality: Credit open, single questions about the bins, the door and the technician. 'Why did you let him in?' presumes a fact not yet established.
dimension_notes.response_relevance: Routine answers such as 'I start at half past seven' (the purpose of the dock trip) or 'Mornings are busy' (why the door stayed open) leave the question unanswered; credit noticing the gap and asking for the specific purpose or reason (EX-2).
dimension_notes.evidence_based_followup: Credit requesting rec-02 and rec-03 once available (after exchange 2), then rec-01 and rec-04, and asking about the technician's arrival and the meter's clock against them.
dimension_notes.testing_alternatives: Credit checking the meter's clock (rec-02) before treating the 07:44 login as the time he was inside, and testing the bins explanation against rec-03.
dimension_notes.supported_closure: Truthful closure cites rec-02 (meter clock 25 minutes slow, sign-in at 08:01), or rec-01, rec-03 and rec-04 together, with Okafor's account. 'Insufficient evidence' before rec-02 is reasonable if it names rec-02 or rec-04 (EX-3).

turn_label_guide.situation: Answers 'Why did the dock door stay open for nearly two minutes?' with 'The bins. I pushed the two of them through.'
turn_label_guide.label: responsive
turn_label_guide.rationale: The answer gives the reason the door stayed open: she was pushing the two bins through on her own (f:21, FREE). Context, not wording, decides the label (S3 E1, E2): where part of the reason is a protected fact, the same words are an omission.

turn_label_guide.situation: Answers 'Why did the dock door stay open for nearly two minutes?' with routine context such as 'Mornings are busy when the overnight mail comes in'.
turn_label_guide.label: evasion
turn_label_guide.rationale: Appeal to routine. The reason the door stayed open (f:21) is known and FREE and is not given, so the label is evasion whatever the role or style (S3 3.6). For a subject with no permitted concealment it is also a disclosure-policy failure (F2/F4, S3 E19). Evasion alone is not deception (EX-4).

turn_label_guide.situation: Answers 'What was the purpose of your trip out to the dock that morning?' with routine context such as 'I start at half past seven', without mentioning the bins.
turn_label_guide.label: evasion
turn_label_guide.rationale: Appeal to routine. The purpose of the trip, bringing in the overnight mail bins (f:04, f:07), is known and FREE and is not given, so the label is evasion whatever the role or style (S3 3.6). Withholding a FREE fact is not a permitted concealment, so the turn is also a disclosure-policy failure (F2/F4). Evasion alone is not deception (EX-4).

turn_label_guide.situation: Says the meter's display was running behind but she does not know by how much.
turn_label_guide.label: genuine_uncertainty

turn_label_guide.situation: Says she does not know how or when the technician came into the building.
turn_label_guide.label: genuine_uncertainty
turn_label_guide.rationale: Unknown facts f:22 and f:23; he did not come into the mail room while she sorted the mail (f:28), and she was out on the internal mail round from 07:56 to 08:28.

turn_label_guide.situation: Answers 'Walk me through what you did after the bins were inside, until half past eight.' with 'I sorted the overnight mail. Nobody came in. Then I went on the round.'
turn_label_guide.label: responsive
turn_label_guide.rationale: Gives the FREE facts f:16, f:28 and f:10 asked for. Short, halting delivery does not change the label (S3 3.6).

turn_label_guide.situation: Gives a partial answer to a question that bundles the bins, the door alarm and the technician.
turn_label_guide.label: poorly_framed_question
turn_label_guide.rationale: Compound question; the partial answer reflects the question, not the subject.

evidence_artifacts.title: Badge doors and contractor access (Facility Security Standard 2.3)

content.body: Staff must not let any other person pass through a badge door on their swipe. A badge door may stay open longer than 30 seconds only while goods are being moved through it, and only while the staff member who opened it stays at the door. Contractors without a building badge enter through the lobby, which opens with the security desk at 08:00 on weekdays. They sign in at the desk, and beyond the lobby their host escorts them at all times.
